questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: What is the frequency of the electron in the first orbit of hydrogen atom of orbital radius $0.5 \times 10^{-10}$ m, if its orbital velocity in that orbit is $2.2 \times 10^6\ ms^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The frequency $ u$ of the electron in its circular orbit is given by the formula:

$ u = \dfrac{v}{2\pi r}$

Substituting the given values $v = 2.2 imes 10^6 ext{ ms}^{-1}$ and $r = 0.5 imes 10^{-10} ext{ m}$:

$ u = \dfrac{2.2 imes 10^6}{2 imes \pi imes 0.5 imes 10^{-10}}$

$ u = \dfrac{2.2 imes 10^6}{\pi imes 10^{-10}}$

$ u = \dfrac{2.2}{\pi} imes 10^{16}$

Using $\pi \approx 3.14$:

$ u \approx \dfrac{2.2}{3.14} imes 10^{16} \approx 0.70 imes 10^{16} ext{ Hz}$

$ u \approx 7.0 imes 10^{15} ext{ Hz}$

Answer : $7.0 imes 10^{15}$ Hz.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A hydrogen atom absorbs energy and rises to n = 3 state from its ground state n = 1. If the potential energy of the atom at its ground state is -13.6eV, find the wave length emitted by it when it returns to its ground state:
{Planck's constant= $6.6 \times 10^{34}$ J s}
questions.solution:
Total energy of hydrogen atom in ground state, $E_1 = -13.6$ eV

Energy in $n=3$ state, $E_3 = \dfrac{-13.6}{3^2} = -1.51$ eV

Energy of emitted photon, $\Delta E = E_3 - E_1 = -1.51 - (-13.6) = 12.09$ eV

Wavelength of emitted photon, $\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E}$

$\lambda = \dfrac{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8}{12.09 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}$

$\lambda = \dfrac{19.8 \times 10^{-26}}{19.34 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 1.023 \times 10^{-7}$ m

$\lambda \approx 1023 Å \approx 1020 Å$

Answer: $1020Å$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An atom with one electron has ionization energy of 24 eV. An electron in this atom makes a transition from an excited energy level, where E = -15 eV, to the ground state. What is the wavelength of the emitted photon from this transition?
questions.solution:
The ionization energy of the atom is $24\ \text{eV}$, which means the energy of the ground state is $E_1 = -24\ \text{eV}$.

The energy of the excited state is given as $E_2 = -15\ \text{eV}$.

When the electron transitions from the excited state to the ground state, the energy of the emitted photon is:

$\Delta E = E_2 - E_1$

$\Delta E = -15\ \text{eV} - (-24\ \text{eV}) = 9\ \text{eV}$

The wavelength of the emitted photon is given by:

$\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E}$

Using $hc \approx 1242\ \text{eV}\cdot\text{nm}$:

$\lambda = \dfrac{1242\ \text{eV}\cdot\text{nm}}{9\ \text{eV}} = 138\ \text{nm}$

Answer: $138\ \text{nm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An atom has a single electron. Its ground state energy is $-30\ eV$ and its first excited state energy is $-8\ eV$. The atom is bombarded with a stream of photons, each of energy $15\ eV$. Assuming the atom being in the ground state, which of the following statements is correct?
options: Atom gets excited to the first excited state and later emit photons of $22\ eV$
Atom absorbs energy continuously until $22\ eV$ is accumulated and then gets excited
Atom will not get excited, and the transmitted light will have the same frequency as the incident light
Atom will absorb the photon and re-emit a photon of lower energy
questions.solution:
The energy of the atom in the ground state is $E_1 = -30\ eV$.

The energy of the atom in the first excited state is $E_2 = -8\ eV$.

The minimum energy required to excite the atom from the ground state to the first excited state is $\Delta E = E_2 - E_1 = -8\ eV - (-30\ eV) = 22\ eV$.

The energy of the incident photon is $15\ eV$.

For an atom to absorb a photon, the photon's energy must exactly match the energy difference between two states of the atom, or it must be greater than the ionization energy (which is $30\ eV$).

Since the incident photon energy (15\ eV$) is less than the minimum excitation energy (22\ eV$), the atom cannot absorb the photon.

Therefore, the atom will not get excited, and the photons will pass through without being absorbed. The transmitted light will have the same frequency as the incident light.

Answer: Atom will not get excited, and the transmitted light will have the same frequency as the incident light

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The ratio of the speed of electron in the $4^{\text{th }}$ orbit of $\mathrm{Li}^{++}$ to the speed of electron in the ground state of hydrogen atom will be:
questions.solution:
The speed of an electron in the $n^{th}$ orbit of a hydrogen-like atom with atomic number $Z$ is given by the formula $v_n = v_0 \dfrac{Z}{n}$, where $v_0$ is the speed of an electron in the ground state of the hydrogen atom ($Z=1, n=1$).

For the $4^{th}$ orbit of $\text{Li}^{++}$, the atomic number $Z = 3$ and the orbit number $n = 4$.

The speed of the electron in this orbit is $v_{Li} = v_0 \dfrac{3}{4}$.

The speed of the electron in the ground state of the hydrogen atom is $v_H = v_0 \dfrac{1}{1} = v_0$.

The ratio of the speed of the electron in the $4^{th}$ orbit of $\text{Li}^{++}$ to the speed of the electron in the ground state of the hydrogen atom is $\dfrac{v_{Li}}{v_H} = \dfrac{v_0 \times \dfrac{3}{4}}{v_0} = \dfrac{3}{4}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{3}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If an electron from a hydrogen like atom with $Z=2$ jumps from the $4^{\text{th }}$ orbit to the $2^{\text{nd }}$ orbit, it emits a photon of wavelength $\lambda$. What is the wavelength of the photon emitted if an electron jumps from the $5^{\text{th }}$ orbit to the $4^{\text{th }}$ orbit?
questions.solution:
The wavelength $\lambda$ of a photon emitted during a transition from orbit $n_2 to n_1$ in a hydrogen-like atom with atomic number $Z$ is given by the Rydberg formula:

$\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R Z^2 \left( \dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2} \right)

For the first case, $ Z=2$, $n_1=2$, and $n_2=4$. Substituting these values:

\dfrac{1}{\lambda} =$ R (2)^2 $\left( \dfrac{1}{2^2} - \dfrac{1}{4^2} \right) =4R \left( \dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{16} \right) =4R \left( \dfrac{4-1}{16} \right) =4R \left( \dfrac{3}{16} \right) = \dfrac{3R}{4}

Thus, $\lambda = $\dfrac{4}{3R}.

For$ the second case, Z=2$, $n_1=4$, and $n_2=5$. Let the wavelength be $\lambda'$.

\dfrac{1}{\lambda'} =$ R (2)^2 $\left( \dfrac{1}{4^2} - \dfrac{1}{5^2} \right) =4R \left( \dfrac{1}{16} - \dfrac{1}{25} \right) =4R \left( \dfrac{25-16}{400} \right) =4R \left( \dfrac{9}{400} \right) = \dfrac{9R}{100}

Thus, $\lambda' = $\dfrac{100}{9R}.

Taking$ the $ratio \dfrac{\lambda'}{\lambda}:

\dfrac{\lambda'}{\lambda} = \dfrac{100}{9R} \times \dfrac{3R}{4} = \dfrac{100 \times 3}{9 \times 4} = \dfrac{300}{36} = \dfrac{25}{3}

Therefore,$\lambda' = $\dfrac{25}{3} \lambda.

Answer: \dfrac{25}{3}$ \lambda

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: What is the frequency ' $v$ ' of the electron in Bohr's first orbit of radius ' $r$ ' of the hydrogen atom?
questions.solution:
For $n=1$, Bohr's quantization gives: $mv_{orb}r = \dfrac{h}{2\pi}$ ... (1)

Electrostatic force provides centripetal force: $\dfrac{mv_{orb}^2}{r} = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2}$ ... (2)

Dividing (2) by (1):
$\dfrac{v_{orb}}{r^2} = \dfrac{e^2 \cdot 2\pi}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2 h}$

$v_{orb} = \dfrac{e^2}{2\epsilon_0 h}$

Frequency of revolution: $v = \dfrac{v_{orb}}{2\pi r} = \dfrac{e^2}{2\epsilon_0 h \cdot 2\pi r} = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 hr}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: What is the kinetic energy of the electron in the nth level, moving in a plane under the influence of a magnetic field 'B'? [ m-mass of electron; h- Planck's constant; e- electronic charge]
questions.solution:
The electron moves in a circular orbit under the influence of a magnetic field $B$. The magnetic force provides the necessary centripetal force for circular motion:

$evB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$

This simplifies to $evB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} \Rightarrow r = \dfrac{mv}{eB}$

According to Bohr's quantization condition for angular momentum:

$mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$

Substituting the expression for $r$ into the quantization condition:

$mv \left( \dfrac{mv}{eB} \right) = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$

$\dfrac{m^2 v^2}{eB} = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$

$m^2 v^2 = \dfrac{nheB}{2\pi}$

$v^2 = \dfrac{nheB}{2\pi m^2}$

The kinetic energy $K$ is given by:

$K = \dfrac{1}{2} mv^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} m \left( \dfrac{nheB}{2\pi m^2} \right)

$K = $\dfrac{nheB}{4\pi m}

Answer: \dfrac{n h e B}{4 \pi m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The minimum energy required by a hydrogen atom in ground state to emit radiation in Paschen series is nearly:
questions.solution:
The energy levels of a hydrogen atom are given by $E_n = -\dfrac{13.6}{n^2} \text{ eV}$.

The Paschen series corresponds to transitions where the electron falls to the energy level $n_f = 3$.

To emit radiation in the Paschen series, the electron must first be excited from the ground state (n_i = 1$) to an excited state $n_e$ such that it can subsequently transition to $n_f = 3$. The lowest energy transition in the Paschen series originates from $n_e = 4$ to $n_f = 3$.

Therefore, the minimum energy required to excite the electron from the ground state (n=1$) to the state $n=4$ is given by $\Delta E = E_4 - E_1$.

$\Delta E = -\dfrac{13.6}{4^2} - (-\dfrac{13.6}{1^2}) = -\dfrac{13.6}{16} + 13.6 = 13.6 \times (1 - 0.0625) = 13.6 \times 0.9375 = 12.75 \text{ eV}$.

Answer: 12.75 eV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Which of the following is correct in the case of the Bohr model of atoms?
A. Predicts continuous emission spectra for all atoms
B. Assumes that the angular momentum of electrons is quantised
C. Predicts same emission spectrum for singly ionised neon atom and hydrogen atom
D. Predicts same emission spectrum for singly ionised neon atom and singly ionised helium atom
questions.solution:
The Bohr model of the atom is based on several postulates, one of which is the quantization of angular momentum. According to this postulate, the angular momentum $L$ of an electron revolving in a stable orbit is an integral multiple of $\dfrac{h}{2\pi}$, expressed as $L = n\dfrac{h}{2\pi}$, where $n$ is an integer.

Regarding the other options: The Bohr model predicts line spectra, not continuous spectra, for hydrogen-like atoms. The emission spectrum depends on the atomic number $Z$, as the energy levels are given by $E_n = -13.6 \dfrac{Z^2}{n^2}$ eV. Since hydrogen ($Z=1$) and singly ionised neon ($Z=10$) have different atomic numbers, their emission spectra are different. Similarly, singly ionised neon ($Z=10$) and singly ionised helium ($Z=2$) have different atomic numbers and thus different spectra.

Answer: B

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: According to Bohr's theory of hydrogen atom, the speed of the electron, its energy and radius of its orbit vary with the principal quantum number n , respectively as
questions.solution:
According to Bohr's theory for a hydrogen-like atom, the radius of the $n^{th}$ orbit is given by $r_n = a_0 \dfrac{n^2}{Z}$, which implies $r_n \propto n^2$.

The velocity of the electron in the $n^{th}$ orbit is given by $v_n = v_0 \dfrac{Z}{n}$, which implies $v_n \propto \dfrac{1}{n}$.

The total energy of the electron in the $n^{th}$ orbit is given by $E_n = -13.6 \dfrac{Z^2}{n^2}$ eV, which implies $E_n \propto \dfrac{1}{n^2}$.

Comparing these dependencies, the speed varies as $\dfrac{1}{n}$, energy varies as $\dfrac{1}{n^2}$, and radius varies as $n^2$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{n}, \dfrac{1}{n^2}, n^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Which, of the following is true of the Balmer series of the hydrogen spectrum?
a. The series is in the visible region.
b. The entire series falls in the ultraviolet region
c. The entire series falls in the infrared region
d. The series is partly in the visible region and partly in the infrared region
questions.solution:
The wavelength of spectral lines in the hydrogen spectrum is given by the Rydberg formula: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R \left( \dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2} \right)$, where $R$ is the Rydberg constant, $n_1$ is the lower energy level, and $n_2$ is the higher energy level.

For the Balmer series, $n_1 = 2$ and $n_2 = 3, 4, 5, \dots$.

The transitions for the Balmer series are as follows:
For $n_2 = 3$, $\lambda = 656.3$ nm (red light).
For $n_2 = 4$, $\lambda = 486.1$ nm (blue-green light).
For $n_2 = 5$, $\lambda = 434.0$ nm (violet light).
For $n_2 = 6$, $\lambda = 410.2$ nm (violet light).
As $n_2 \to \infty$, the series limit is $\lambda = 364.6$ nm.

Since all these wavelengths fall within the range of approximately $380$ nm to $750$ nm, the entire Balmer series lies in the visible region of the electromagnetic spectrum.

Answer: a

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Calculate the radius of the second Bohr's orbit of electron of hydrogen atom.
questions.solution:
Radius of the $n$th Bohr's orbit of the hydrogen atom is given by
$\begin{aligned} \\ r_n & =\frac{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 n^2 h^2}{4 \pi^2 m e^2} \\ \\ r_2 & =\frac{4 \pi \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times(2)^2 \times\left(6.625 \times 10^{-34}\right)^2}{4 \pi^2 \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right)^2} \\ \\ & =\frac{8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 4 \times\left(6.625 \times 10^{-34}\right)^2}{\pi \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right)^2} \\ \\ & =2.12 \times 10^{-10} \mathrm{ m} \\ \\ & =2.12 \\ \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a helium ion, if potential energy of electron in ground state is assumed to be zero, then its energy in first excited state is equal to
questions.solution: Potential energy of a $\mathrm{He}^{+}$ ion in ground state is$\begin{aligned} \\ & U_1=2 E_1=2\left(-13.6 \frac{Z^2}{n^2}\right) \\ \\ & \because \quad n=1 \text{ and } Z=2 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \quad U_1=-108.8 \mathrm{eV} \\ \end{aligned}$But PE in ground state is given zero. So, we have to increase PE (and total energy) by 108.8 eV .Hence, for given $\mathrm{He}^{+}$ ion, energy of first excited state $(n=2)$ will be$\begin{aligned} \\ E(n=2) & =-13.6 \frac{Z^2}{n^2}+108.8 \\ \\ & =-13.6 \times \frac{4}{4}+108.8 \\ \\ & =95.2 \mathrm{eV} \\ \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The minimum radial distance between first orbit and second orbit in $\mathrm{He}^{+}$ ion, if the de-Broglie wavelength of an electron in first orbit is $\lambda$, will be
questions.solution: By de-Broglie hypothesis,$2 \pi r_n=n \lambda$For first orbit, $n=1, r=r_1$, then$2 \pi r_1=\lambda \text{$ or $} r_1=\frac{\lambda}{2 \pi}$For second orbit, $n=2, r=r_2$, then$\begin{aligned} \\ 2 \pi r_2 & =2 \lambda \\ \\ \text{or } r_2 & =\frac{2 \lambda}{2 \pi} \\ \end{aligned}$Minimum radial distance between first orbit and second orbit is$\begin{aligned} \\ & r_2-r_1=\frac{2 \lambda}{2 \pi}-\frac{\lambda}{2 \pi} \\ \\ \Rightarrow \quad & r_2-r_1=\frac{\lambda}{2 \pi} \\ \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The shortest wavelengths of Paschen, Lymen and Balmer series are in the ratio
questions.solution:
The wavelength $\lambda$ for a transition in a hydrogen-like atom is given by the Rydberg formula: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R Z^2 \left( \dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2} \right).

For the shortest wavelength of any series, the transition occurs from $n_2 = $\infty$ to n_1$. Thus, \dfrac{1}{\lambda_{min}} =$R $\left( \dfrac{1}{n_1^2} \right)$, which implies $\lambda_{min} = \dfrac{n_1^2}{R}$.

For the Paschen series, $n_1 = 3$, so $\lambda_{Paschen} = \dfrac{3^2}{R} = \dfrac{9}{R}$.

For the Lyman series, $n_1 = 1$, so $\lambda_{Lyman} = \dfrac{1^2}{R} = \dfrac{1}{R}$.

For the Balmer series, $n_1 = 2$, so $\lambda_{Balmer} = \dfrac{2^2}{R} = \dfrac{4}{R}$.

The ratio of the shortest wavelengths of Paschen, Lyman, and Balmer series is $\lambda_{Paschen} : \lambda_{Lyman} : \lambda_{Balmer} = \dfrac{9}{R} : \dfrac{1}{R} : \dfrac{4}{R} = 9 : 1 : 4$.

Answer: $9: 1: 4$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a hydrogen atom, if electron is replaced by a particle which is 40 times heavier but has the same charge, then, the ratio of the radius of the first excited state of a normal hydrogen atom to the ground state of the above atom is
questions.solution:
The radius of the $n$-th orbit of a hydrogen-like atom is given by $r_n = \dfrac{n^2 a_0}{Z} \times \dfrac{m_e}{m}$, where $m$ is the mass of the particle and $a_0$ is the Bohr radius of the hydrogen atom ($a_0 = \dfrac{h^2}{4\pi^2 m_e e^2}$).

For a normal hydrogen atom, $m = m_e$, $Z = 1$, and the first excited state corresponds to $n = 2$. Thus, $r_{H} = \dfrac{2^2 a_0}{1} = 4 a_0$.

For the new atom, the particle mass is $m' = 40 m_e$, $Z = 1$, and the ground state corresponds to $n = 1$. Thus, $r' = \dfrac{1^2}{1} \times \dfrac{m_e}{40 m_e} a_0 = \dfrac{a_0}{40}$.

The ratio of the radius of the first excited state of the normal hydrogen atom to the ground state of the new atom is $\dfrac{r_H}{r'} = \dfrac{4 a_0}{a_0 / 40} = 4 \times 40 = 160$.

Therefore, the ratio is $160 : 1$.

Answer: 160 : 1

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If an electron in a hydrogen atom jumps from the third orbit to the second orbit, it emits a photon of wavelength $\lambda$. When it jumps from the second to the first orbit, the corresponding wavelength of the photon will be
questions.solution:
The Rydberg formula for the wavelength of a photon emitted during an electronic transition in a hydrogen atom is given by $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R \left( \dfrac{1}{n_f^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_i^2} \right), where $ R$ is the Rydberg constant.

For the transition from the third orbit ($n_i = 3$) to the second orbit ($n_f = 2$), the wavelength $\lambda$ is given by:
\dfrac{1}{\lambda} =$ R $\left( \dfrac{1}{2^2} - \dfrac{1}{3^2} \right) =$ R $\left( \dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{9} \right) =$ R $\left( \dfrac{9 - 4}{36} \right) = \dfrac{5R}{36}

For$ the transition from the second orbit ( n_i = 2$) to the first orbit ($n_f = 1$), let the wavelength be $\lambda'$. Then:
\dfrac{1}{\lambda'} =$ R $\left( \dfrac{1}{1^2} - \dfrac{1}{2^2} \right) =$ R $\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{4} \right) = \dfrac{3R}{4}

Dividing$ the $two expressions:
\dfrac{\lambda'}{\lambda} = \dfrac{5R/36}{3R/4} = \dfrac{5}{36} \times \dfrac{4}{3} = \dfrac{5}{27}

Therefore,$\lambda' = $\dfrac{5 \lambda}{27}.

Answer: \dfrac{5 \lambda}{27}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The distance of closest approach when an alpha particle of kinetic energy $6.5 \text{ MeV}$ strikes a nucleus of atomic number 50 is
questions.solution:
At closest approach, KE = PE:

$r_0 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \cdot \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{K}$

$q_1 = 2e$, $q_2 = 50e$, $K = 6.5$ MeV $= 6.5 \times 10^6 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ J

$r_0 = \dfrac{(9 \times 10^9) \times 100 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})}{6.5 \times 10^6}$

$= \dfrac{9 \times 10^{11} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{6.5 \times 10^6}$

$= \dfrac{14.4 \times 10^{-8}}{6.5 \times 10^6} = 2.215 \times 10^{-14}$ m

$= 0.0221$ pm

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electron has a mass of $9.1 \times 10^{-31} \mathrm{ kg}$. It revolves round the nucleus in a circular orbit of radius $0.529 \times 10^{-10} \mathrm{ m}$ at a speed of $2.2 \times 10^6 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$. The magnitude of its angular momentum is
questions.solution:
The angular momentum $L$ of a particle moving in a circular orbit is given by the formula $L = mvr$, where $m$ is the mass of the particle, $v$ is its speed, and $r$ is the radius of the orbit.

Given values are:
$m = 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$
$v = 2.2 \times 10^{6} \text{ ms}^{-1}$
$r = 0.529 \times 10^{-10} \text{ m}$

Substituting these values into the formula:
$L = (9.1 \times 10^{-31}) \times (2.2 \times 10^{6}) \times (0.529 \times 10^{-10})$

Calculating the product of the numerical coefficients:
$9.1 \times 2.2 \times 0.529 = 20.02 \times 0.529 \approx 10.59 \approx 10.6$

Calculating the power of 10:
$10^{-31} \times 10^{6} \times 10^{-10} = 10^{-31 + 6 - 10} = 10^{-35}$

Combining these results:
$L = 10.6 \times 10^{-35} \text{ kg m}^2 \texts^{-1}$
$L = 1.06 \times 10^{-34} \text{ kg m}^2 \texts^{-1}$

Answer: $1.06 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{Kg} \mathrm{m}^2 \mathrm{ s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The difference in energy levels of an electron at two excited levels is $13.75 \mathrm{ eV}$. If it makes a transition from the higher energy level to the lower energy level then what will be the wave length of the emitted radiation?
[given $h=6.6 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{ m}^2 \mathrm{ kg} \mathrm{ s}^{-1} ; c=3 \times 10^8 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1} ; 1 \mathrm{ eV}=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{ J}$]
questions.solution:
The energy difference between the two levels is given by $\Delta E = 13.75 \text{ eV}$.

Converting this energy into Joules:
$\Delta E = 13.75 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J} = 22 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$.

The relationship between energy and wavelength is $\Delta E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$.

Rearranging for wavelength $\lambda$:
$\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E}$.

Substituting the given values $h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$ and $c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}$:
$\lambda = \dfrac{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8}{22 \times 10^{-19}}$.

$\lambda = \dfrac{19.8 \times 10^{-26}}{22 \times 10^{-19}} = 0.9 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$.

Converting to Angstroms ($\text{A}$):
$\lambda = 0.9 \times 10^{-7} \times 10^{10} \text{ A} = 0.9 \times 10^3 \text{ A} = 900 \text{ A}$.

Answer: $900^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{A}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The wavelength of the first line of Lyman series for $\mathrm{H}$ - atom is equal to that of the second line of Balmer series for a $\mathrm{H}$-like ion. The atomic number $\mathrm{Z}$ of $\mathrm{H}$-like ion is
questions.solution:
Lyman series of $\mathrm{H}$-atom, we can write
$\frac{h c}{\lambda}=R h c \left(\frac{1}{1^2}-\frac{1}{2^2}\right)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In the head-on collision of two alpha particles $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ with the gold nucleus, the closest approaches are 31.4 fermi and 94.2 fermi respectively. Then the ratio of the energy possessed by the alpha particles $\alpha_2 / \alpha_1$ is:
questions.solution:
The distance of closest approach $r_0$ for an alpha particle of kinetic energy $K$ colliding head-on with a nucleus of atomic number $Z$ is given by the formula $r_0 = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0} \dfrac{2Ze^2}{K}$.

From this expression, it is evident that $r_0 \propto \dfrac{1}{K}$, which implies $K \propto \dfrac{1}{r_0}$.

Given the closest approaches for the two alpha particles are $r_1 = 31.4$ fermi and $r_2 = 94.2$ fermi, the ratio of their kinetic energies $K_2 / K_1$ is given by:

$\dfrac{K_2}{K_1} = \dfrac{r_1}{r_2}$

Substituting the given values:

$\dfrac{K_2}{K_1} = \dfrac{31.4}{94.2} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Answer: $1: 3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The ground state energy of hydrogen atom is $-13.6 \mathrm{ eV} . If the electron jumps from the $3^{$\text{rd }$}$ excited state to the ground state then the energy of the radiation emitted will be:$
questions.solution:
The energy of an electron in the $n^{th}$ orbit of a hydrogen atom is given by $E_n = -\dfrac{13.6}{n^2} \text{ eV}$.

The ground state corresponds to $n = 1$. The $3^{rd}$ excited state corresponds to $n = 1 + 3 = 4$.

The energy of the electron in the ground state is $E_1 = -\dfrac{13.6}{1^2} = -13.6 \text{ eV}$.

The energy of the electron in the $3^{rd}$ excited state is $E_4 = -\dfrac{13.6}{4^2} = -\dfrac{13.6}{16} = -0.85 \text{ eV}$.

When the electron jumps from the $3^{rd}$ excited state (n=4$) to the ground state (n=1$), the energy of the emitted radiation is given by $\Delta E = E_4 - E_1$.

$\Delta E = -0.85 - (-13.6) = 13.6 - 0.85 = 12.75 \text{ eV}$.

Answer: 12.75 eV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The first emission of hydrogen atomic spectrum in Lyman series appears at a wavelength of
questions.solution:
The Rydberg formula for the hydrogen spectrum is given by $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R \left( \dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2} \right), where $ R$ is the Rydberg constant.

For the Lyman series, the transition occurs to the ground state, so $n_1 = 1$. The first emission line corresponds to the transition from the first excited state, $n_2 = 2.

Substituting these values into the $formula:

\dfrac{1}{\lambda} =$ R $\left( \dfrac{1}{1^2} - \dfrac{1}{2^2} \right) =$ R $\left( 1 - \dfrac{1}{4} \right) = R \left( \dfrac{3}{4} \right)

Therefore,$ the wavelength\lambda$ is given by:

$\lambda = $\dfrac{4}{3R} \text{ cm}

Answer: \dfrac{4}{3 R} \mathrm{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The wavelength of the first line of Lyman series for $\mathrm{H}$ - atom is equal to that of the second line of Balmer series for a $\mathrm{H}$-like ion. The atomic number $\mathrm{Z}$ of $\mathrm{H}$-like ion is
questions.solution:
The wavelength $\lambda$ for a transition in a hydrogen-like ion is given by the Rydberg formula: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R Z^2 \left( \dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2} \right).

For the first line of the Lyman series in H-atom ($ Z=1$): $n_1 = 1$, $n_2 = 2$.
\dfrac{1}{\lambda_1} =$ R(1)^2 $\left( \dfrac{1}{1^2} - \dfrac{1}{2^2} \right) =$ R $\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{4} \right) = \dfrac{3R}{4}.

For$ the second line of the Balmer series in a H-like ion with atomic number Z$: $n_1 = 2$, $n_2 = 4$.
\dfrac{1}{\lambda_2} =$ R Z² $\left( \dfrac{1}{2^2} - \dfrac{1}{4^2} \right) =$ R Z² $\left( \dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{16} \right) =$ R Z² $\left( \dfrac{4-1}{16} \right) = \dfrac{3R Z^2}{16}.

Equating$ the wavelengths\lambda_1 = \lambda_2$, we have \dfrac{1}{\lambda_1} = \dfrac{1}{\lambda_2}.
\dfrac{3R}{4} = \dfrac{3R Z^2}{16}.

Simplifying$ the $equation:
\dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{Z^2}{16} \Rightarrow$ Z^2 = 4 \Rightarrow Z = 2$.

Answer: 2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which of the following series spectrum of hydrogen atom lies in ultraviolet region?
questions.solution:
The wavelength $\lambda$ of the spectral lines in the hydrogen atom is given by the Rydberg formula: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R \left( \dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2} \right), where $ n_1$ is the lower energy level and $n_2$ is the higher energy level.

For the Lyman series, $n_1 = 1$ and $n_2 = 2, 3, 4, \dots$. The transitions to the ground state ($n_1 = 1$) involve large energy differences, which correspond to the ultraviolet region of the electromagnetic spectrum.

For the Balmer series, $n_1 = 2$, which lies in the visible region.

For the Paschen series, $n_1 = 3$, which lies in the infrared region.

For the Brackett series, $n_1 = 4$, which lies in the infrared region.

For the Pfund series, $n_1 = 5$, which lies in the infrared region.

Therefore, the Lyman series is the only one among the given options that lies in the ultraviolet region.

Answer: Lyman series$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The wavelength of the second line of Balmer series is $486.4 \mathrm{ nm}$. What is the wavelength of the first line of Lyman series?
questions.solution:
The Rydberg formula for the wavelength $\lambda$ of a spectral line in a hydrogen-like atom is given by $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R \left( \dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2} \right) Z^2$. For hydrogen, $Z = 1$.

The second line of the Balmer series corresponds to the transition from $n_2 = 4 to n_1 = 2$. Thus, $\dfrac{1}{\lambda_B} = R \left( \dfrac{1}{2^2} - \dfrac{1}{4^2} \right) = R \left( \dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{16} \right) =$ R $\left( \dfrac{3}{16} \right). Given $\lambda_B = 486.4 $\text{ nm}, we have $ R = $\dfrac{16}{3 \times 486.4} \text{ nm}^{-1}.

The first line$ of the Lyman series corresponds to the transition from n_2 = 2 to n_1 = 1$. Thus, \dfrac{1}{\lambda_L} =$ R $\left( \dfrac{1}{1^2} - \dfrac{1}{2^2} \right) =$ R $\left( 1 - \dfrac{1}{4} \right) = R \left( \dfrac{3}{4} \right).

Substituting$ the value of R$: \dfrac{1}{\lambda_L} = \left( \dfrac{16}{3 \times 486.4} \right) \times \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{4}{486.4} = \dfrac{1}{121.6}.

Therefore, $\lambda_L = 121.6 $\text{ nm}.

Answer: 121.6 \mathrm{ nm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The Lyman series of a hydrogen atom belongs in which category
questions.solution:
The energy levels of a hydrogen atom are given by the Rydberg formula: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R \left( \dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2} \right), where $ R$ is the Rydberg constant, $n_1$ is the lower energy level, and $n_2$ is the higher energy level.

For the Lyman series, the electron transitions occur to the ground state, which corresponds to $n_1 = 1$. The transitions are from $n_2 = 2, 3, 4, \dots$.

The energy difference \Delta$ E = E_{n_2} - E_1$ for these transitions is very large, falling in the range of ultraviolet radiation. Therefore, the Lyman series lies in the ultraviolet region of the electromagnetic spectrum.

Answer: ultraviolet region$

questions.solution:
The frequency $ u$ of the radiation emitted when an electron jumps from an energy level $n_2$ to $n_1$ is given by the Rydberg formula:

$ u = R c \left( \dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2} ight)

u = R c \left( \dfrac{1}{2^2} - \dfrac{1}{3^2} ight)$

$ u = R c \left( \dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{9} ight)$

$ u = R c \left( \dfrac{9 - 4}{36} ight)$

$ u = \dfrac{5 R c}{36}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
options: Classical Physics deals with macroscopic phenomena and includes subject like mechanics, electrodynamics, optics and thermodynamics.
All Physics and also mathematics is based on assumptions each of which is variously called hypothesis or axiom or postulate etc.
A hypothesis is a supposition with asstuming that is true.
An axiom is a self-evident truth, while a modei is a theory proposed to explain observed phenomena.
questions.solution:
Classical physics is indeed concerned with macroscopic phenomena, encompassing mechanics, electrodynamics, optics, and thermodynamics, making the first statement correct.

Physics and mathematics are built upon foundational assumptions known as hypotheses, axioms, or postulates, which serve as the starting points for logical deduction, making the second statement correct.

An axiom is defined as a self-evident truth or a starting assumption accepted without proof, and a model is a theoretical framework used to explain observed phenomena, making the fourth statement correct.

A hypothesis is a tentative supposition or a proposed explanation made on the basis of limited evidence as a starting point for further investigation, not necessarily assuming it is true. The statement that a hypothesis is a supposition with assuming that it is true is conceptually incorrect as it implies a lack of testing or verification, which is the core of the scientific method.

Answer: A hypothesis is a supposition with asstuming that is true.

questions.q: $Which state of triply ionised Beryllium  \left(\mathrm{Be}^{+++}\right) has the same orbital radius as that of the ground state of hydrogen?$
questions.solution:
Radius of $n$ th-orbit in hydrogen like atom is given by $r=\frac{n^{2} h^{2}}{4 \pi^{2} m k Z e^{2}}$
i.e., $\quad r \propto \frac{n^{2}}{Z}$
For hydrogen, $Z=1, n=1$ in ground state $\Rightarrow \quad \frac{n^{2}}{Z}=\frac{1^{2}}{1}=1$
For Beryllium $\left(\mathrm{Be}^{+++}\right), Z=4$ orbital is same
$\therefore \quad \frac{n^{2}}{Z}=1\Rightarrow \quad n^{2}=1 \times Z \Rightarrow n^{2}=4\Rightarrow \quad n=2$
Thus, the second level of triply ionised $\mathrm{Be}^{+++}$has same radius as the ground state of hydrogen.

questions.q: Excitation energy of a hydrogen like ion in its first excitation state is $40.8 \mathrm{eV}$. Energy needed to remove the electron from the ion in ground state is
questions.solution:
Excitation energy of hydrogen like ion in its first excitation state, $\Delta E=40.8 \mathrm{eV}$
For the hydrogen like ion, energy in the ground state $(n=1)$,

E=$\frac{-13.6 Z^{2}}{n^{2}} \mathrm{eV}=-$13.6 Z^{2} $\mathrm{eV}$Energy in the first excited state, $E_{2}=\frac{-13.6 Z^{2}}{n^{2}}$
=$\frac{-13.6 Z^{2}}{4}$Excitation energy, $\Delta E=E_{2}-E_{1} \begin{aligned}$&=$\left(\frac{-13.6 Z^{2}}{4}+$13.6 Z^{2}\right) $\mathrm{eV}$\\
&=(-3.4+13.6) Z^{2} $\mathrm{eV}$\\
\Rightarrow \quad 40.8 $\mathrm{eV}$&=10.2 Z^{2} $\mathrm{eV}$\\
\Rightarrow \quad \quad Z^{2} &=$\frac{40.8}{10.2}$\\
\Rightarrow \quad \quad Z^{2} &=4 \\
\Rightarrow \quad \quad Z &=2
\end{aligned}

Thus, energy$ of the electron in the ground state is given as$\begin{array}{ll}
\Rightarrow& E_{1}=-13.6(2)^{2} $\mathrm{eV}$\\
\Rightarrow & E_{1}=-54.4 $\mathrm{eV}$\end{array}Hence, the $energy needed to remove the electron from the ion in ground state (ionisation energy)

=-(-54.4)\mathrm{eV}=54.4 \mathrm{eV}$
